abstract: This lecture covers the recognition and management of respiratory distress in adults, emphasizing clinical assessment over isolated numbers. Key cases include asthma exacerbation, DKA with compensatory tachypnea, CHF with pulmonary edema, and tension pneumothorax. The speaker reviews oxygen delivery devices, ABG interpretation, and contraindications to BiPAP. Practical pearls include not suppressing compensatory tachypnea, using accessory muscle use as a key sign, and recognizing that a patient's report of being tired of breathing is an indication for ventilation.
key_points: Respiratory rate >30 is concerning; accessory muscle use is a key indicator of distress.
In DKA, tachypnea is compensatory; do not slow it down.
For asthma exacerbation, start with albuterol and reassess before escalating.
In CHF with fluid overload, step up Lasix dose; expect a creatinine bump.
Tension pneumothorax is diagnosed by midline shift, widened rib spaces, and depressed diaphragm; treat with needle decompression.
ABG interpretation: first determine acidotic or alkalotic, then check CO2 and bicarb; use chemistry bicarb not calculated ABG bicarb.
Oxygen delivery: nasal cannula max 6 L/min (~40%), simple mask 5-10 L/min (35-55%), non-rebreather up to 15 L/min (60-95%).
BiPAP contraindications: GCS <7, vomiting, facial trauma, cardiac arrest (absolute); anxiety and inability to protect airway (relative).
Defibrillators can be identified by a coil on the lead; all defibrillators can pace.
A patient saying they are tired of breathing is a strong indication for intubation regardless of numbers.
On BiPAP, FiO2 and EPAP improve oxygenation; the IPAP-EPAP difference determines tidal volume and CO2 clearance.
For a patient with pH 7.2, pCO2 80, O2 50, increase FiO2 and respiratory rate first.
